projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Wolf was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Today is February 11, 2004. I'm interviewing John Wolf, World War II and a Vietnam War vet. Interviewer is Eileen Hurst Downey, Central Connecticut State University. We're interviewing at Central Connecticut State University. John, will you tell me your full name, your birth date and your current address?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: John William Wolf. 66 Emmett Street, Lot 50, Bristol, Tur -- Forestville -- no. What town is this? Forestville. Forestville. Forestville, Connecticut.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And your birth date?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And John, what wars were you in and the branch of the service?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I was in the U.S. Air Force for 25 and a half years or 26 years. I was involved with the -- the Korean War -- not the Korean War, but the -- World War II and Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And what was your rank when you left service?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Master sergeant, U.S. Air Force.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember the year?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember what year you were drafted?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh. I put in 26 years, so it's 1940-something. '44 maybe.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Well, it was during World War II?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I think -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you know how old you were at the time?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Twenty-one, I believe.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: In Newark, New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Why did you pick the branch of the service that you did? The Air Force didn't draft you -- oh, the Air Force was part of the Army then?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. I picked the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Why did you pick the Air Force?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Because I didn't want to be in the Army. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in service?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Did what?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in service?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Did I retire in first --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you recall --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I'm very deaf.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, okay. Do you recall your first days in service? What was it like, the first days that you were in the --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: The first day in service? Well, I was in Camp Dix, New Jersey for about 30 days. Spent 10 of those days on KP, which was -- they say was a outstanding performance. KP, peeling potatoes and -- and all the other stuff that -- cleaning up the pots and pans.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Was this during basic training?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: This is -- first thing in basic training. Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What else did they teach you in basic training besides KP?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Not much at the -- at my first station. I took my basic training at -- in Florida, Miami Beach, Florida. I was there for about six or seven months, just the basic training. We did our basic training right on the beach in Fl -- in Miami.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What kinds of things did they teach you there?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, they just -- most of it was all physical training and checked out how to hold and shoot a rifle. Basic training was mostly all mental stuff. And activities would normally be performed under the Air Force at the time. I think it was in the process of -- in the war and -- I don't know. I think I stayed in Miami Beach about six months, basic training. And --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, no. No. They were just all servicemen, the same like -- I don't remember any of their names or what their -- position they held. I know I was stationed at Dover, Delaware for about five times in my career as aircraft maintenance technician, after going to Keesler Field for four or five months for basic training on aircraft maintenance. Let's see. What else?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: When you were in Miami Beach, what job were you training to do?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It was just basic training, how to be --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: A soldier?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: -- up-to-date serviceman, you know.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Yeah. Where did you go after Miami Beach?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, boy. That's a long time ago. I thought I had all this information at home, but I -- I went through my cabinets last night, and I couldn't find it. Different stations I was -- I was stationed at.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: When did you go overseas?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I went overseas the first time -- I went -- I went to Hickam Field, Hawaii for about four and a half years.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And had the war started?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So you were stationed in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I was stationed in Hawaii. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What was your job assignment?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Aircraft maintenance technician.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What was Hawaii like for the four years you were there?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, it was very quiet at that time. There wasn't that much activity going on from the Japanese. I spent a lot of time on the beach and NCO club. I -- I was a -- ser -- man -- not a manager, but assistant manager of the NCO club after a while and took care of the bartenders and the bars. And before I left there, I was the manager of the NCO club at the Hickam Air Force Base. From there, I can't remember because I was in so many different stations, how many different moves I've made.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: But you can't remember (inaudible)? Did you see combat?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I -- I didn't actually see combat, but I was in -- in Eye-ee-shima (phonetic), Japan during World War II. And there was quite a few times that aircraft come over our huts with shooting, and we had to jump out of our bed and run into a ditch that we all had built -- made before at the time, and we would get down and huddle up in the ditch.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And this was in Japan?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I was -- let's see. I don't think I was ever in Japan. No. I think Vietnam was the closest I got to it.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Can you remember any experiences from World War II? We'll do World War II first and then Vietnam.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. Well, the only thing is -- I can remember is the fact going to aircraft maintenance school and coming out as a -- as a member of the -- of the -- of the maintenance department. And I worked on the -- anywhere from C-54s up to C-124s on different types of maintenance. I was assistant line chief for a while there during the war. Let's see. Where did I go after that? It's been a long time for me to remember.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Well, that was a long time ago.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. The ones I have on.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Can you tell me what those are for?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I would have told you.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: I'll look it up and I'll put it in the record for the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I know that this is a -- this is a good -- service report -- what --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Good Conduct Award --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Good conduct.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- or Good Conduct Medal?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: This is Asia Pacific. This one is -- oh, jeez. What kind of medal is that? Meritorious medal for something. And this one, I forget that. And this one. I don't remember it. If I -- if -- if they didn't go into my stuff this morning, I would have had that book with me. I could tell you exactly what each one --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Well, we'll look it up. Are all of those medals from World War II?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. Every one.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And what was your rank at the time in World War II? Were you a sergeant already?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: In World War II?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, I was a staff sergeant for a long time. And then I finally made master sergeant in 19 -- what does it say in there?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: I think we had that. In 1964.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: While you were in Hawaii, how did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Some places, I was lucky enough to have my family with me, but there were some stations where they -- the families weren't allowed. And if it was close enough -- like I was stationed in Dover, Delaware three or four different times, and I was living in Patterson, New Jersey, and I used to run home once a month on a weekend in Patterson, which is about 120-mile drive for me.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I'm not even sure what time -- what year I got married.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Were you married while you were in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yeah. Hawaii, I was -- and she was with me in -- in China for a while, too.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: You were stationed in China at one time?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. What is it? Nanking. I was in there for about six months, and they gave her permission to come over and visit me for a while.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What were you doing in China? Aircraft maintenance?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Aircraft maintenance technician.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did we have a base there?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. I don't remember the base, though.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember how long you were in China?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Maybe six to eight months, I was in there. And then I -- I think I -- that's another time that I went back to Dover Air Force Base for reassignment again. Stayed there another three or four years. Then they decided to send me someplace else.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Well, you've been a lot of places. You've been around.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yes. I've been -- I've been around the country.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What was the food like in the service?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: The food? I would say it was mediocre food. Sometimes the KP attendants would make -- make things too spicy or things like that. There weren't too many times when we had special me -- special meals like turkey or things like that. Only on special occasions, you'd get a blast of some decent food. But the normal food was potatoes and eggs and -- and sometimes waffles. It was edible, but you know, it was nothing to brag about either.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Why did you decide to make the military your career? If you were drafted, you only had to stay for a few years.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: But you stayed a lot longer than that.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes, I did. Well, at the time, there was no jobs on the outside anyway. And I figured the best place to be would be in the service where I had a steady income. And I raised three children while in the service. I have -- one son is a -- he's a retired captain from the Hartford police department. He retired in -- two or three years ago. He now lives in Florida with his family. My other -- my other children live within driving distance of where I live. My next son, my second son lives in Southington, Connecticut. And I used to go over to see -- over there once or twice a month, just to have something to eat, and some occasion would come up and have a little party. And my daughter, she lives in -- in -- what is it now? I should have had those all -- I'm going -- in fact, I'm going to see her this weekend. And she lives in --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: (laughter) But it's close by?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So you had two boys and a girl?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Two boys and a girl. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you feel pressure or stress while you were in the Air Force?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. Not really.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you do anything for good luck?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: For good luck?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Yes. You know how some guys have rabbit foot?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. Not -- not too much that I can consider good luck.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So you were in World War II. And where were you during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: In the Korean War --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: You must have been stationed in the United States. Were you stationed back home?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I must have been in the United States at the time because I didn't go to Korea at all.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: All right. You skipped the Korean War. And how did you get involved in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: That's a choice of my own to go to Vietnam and help out over there the best I could. But as I said, I was only there a total of ten and a half months or so and then --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Where did you go in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: At -- the name of the base now.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Was it Tan Son Nhut? Tan Son Nhut Air Base was in the south --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. Tan Son Nhut. Yeah. Tan Son Nhut, I was at. Yeah. Yeah. While I was over there, my son was in the -- in the Coast Guard, and his ship was out in the -- in the Vietnam waters. I took a flight down from Tan Son Nhut to -- to another base where I could get a flight -- not a flight, but a ship to take me out to his ship in the Vietnam waters. I spent overnight with my son on his ship. The Navy come back the next morning, picked me up and brought me back to the shore again.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow. That must have been something to be all the way --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- across the world and to see your son.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. That's right.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So your son was in the Coast Guard at the same time you were in the Air Force?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And you were both fighting in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What did that feel like?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, we kept contact with each other because -- he traveled around so much, you know. I never knew where he was at. In the Coast Guard, I guess it's a touch-and-go, how long they stay one place.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Was that the only time that you got to see him while you were in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Just once.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What was your job assignment while you were in Vietnam? Aircraft maintenance?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I was an aircraft maintenance technician. I was a flight chief, and I was a line chief also.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What does a line chief do?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Line chief takes care of assigning different jobs to the maintenance men and perform major inspections on the aircraft. Authorize permission to go on leave when the maintenance men have the time or the reason to go someplace. It was a lot of responsibility as a line chief.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And did you stay right on Tan Son Nhut Air Base when you were over in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yes. I did.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And that's where they would bring the aircraft (inaudible)?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, we only had -- we only had seven aircraft at Tan Son Nhut. And I -- I was -- I wasn't a line chief there. I was chief of the maintenance. I was -- when the planes landed after a mission, the crew chief on that plane would come in and report to me what the -- what went wrong with the airplane. And then I would submit my report to the service personnel. And they would assign different people to go out and repair whatever they wrote up in the book.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: How did the aircraft differ in Vietnam from what you worked out in World War II? You must have had to keep up to date as aircraft evolved.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: When I was -- in Vietnam, I was -- we had C-7As, which was a two-engine carrier, people and -- and material. It was a small airplane, but it was a lively airplane. And they would -- they would take off early in the morning, come back around midnoon sometimes and sometimes later. It all depends on how things were going. When they were transporting things, they would have to go to different -- different stations in the -- in Viet -- Vietnam to deliver things.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Were C-7As considered a cargo plane then?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It was a cargo plane, but it was a converted cargo plane. It could be set up as a passenger plane also. It had -- the metal -- the -- the material that would fold up and just -- just hang up on a hook and as -- as a passenger plane. When they used it as a shuttle plane with material, then they just rolled everything up on rollers that was in the airplane. They'd tie them all down and stock them up so that they wouldn't move while they're going to their destination.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Were all seven aircraft at Tan Son Nhut the C-7As?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. Yes. Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Your entire 10 months in Vietnam, is that the aircraft that you worked on?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. I didn't work on them. I was --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: You were in charge --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I was the chief.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- of the --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- of having other guys work on them.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I did go out and do work on one airplane one day because I hadn't -- nobody that could repair what went wrong. And I worked on the -- one of the engines and had to work in the wheel well to get at the part that was bad. That was quite an experience, too.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It was -- it was a hydraulic thing that I had to replace. It was part of the engine, the hydraulic system, but in order to get at it, you had to go in through a wheel well, take off some cowling, and then the part would be in front of you, and you'd have to have special tools and equipment just to get at the -- at the item that you're going to replace and then take it out and get a new one from supply and put another one back in.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you ever feel pressure or stressed at times like that, that you had to get those aircraft fixed?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Not really any stress. No. As I said, I had one airplane specially that I worked on, and the rest of the time, I spent as the maintenance officer or whatever you want to call it. And I took all the discrepancies from the crew chiefs of these aircraft after they come back from a mission. Then I would call the re -- the report, the maintenance report in to the -- think of what they called it now. Anyway -- anyway, it was the people that were in the maintenance control. Maintenance control. I called maintenance control, and they would assign different sections of -- different stations on the field to go out and repair the part that was -- needed to be repaired.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: How many men would you say worked on aircraft maintenance? Is this a large group or a small?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, I can remember -- I can remember they took a picture of me for some reason, and there was something about 100, 110 men or something. It was the whole flight -- the whole flight -- the whole flight crews. All the people that worked on the airplanes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you make friendships with fellow officers or men?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Friendships?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I had quite a few friend -- fellows that worked for me that we were pretty close, and I probably didn't get to see them as often as I wanted to, but occasionally, I would run into one of them in the NCO club or something like that or in the canteen. And there was -- there wasn't that many people that -- that was over there with their families. I was the luck -- I was one of the lucky ones that had my family there.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Your family was there?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. For a while. My wife was there almost six months before they decided to send her back home.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow. That wasn't dangerous?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It was. Yes. She come home on a ship. It took almost a week or so before the ship got from Cam Rahn Bay to New York.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow. That was a long cruise.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It was a long -- it was a long trip. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Was she there while your son was there, too?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. She wasn't there when my son and I met. I was isolated out there by myself.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: How did your -- did your son enlist or was he drafted?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. I think he enlisted in the Coast Guard. I don't think he got drafted.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you ever leave Tan Son Nhut Air Base and go any other places in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Not -- not legally, no. Not -- not -- not more than a day or so anyway. There was a couple other bases around where some of the members that were stationed there were maintenance men I had known for years. And I'd -- I'd hitch a ride down in one of the C-7As and go down to visit my friends and come back the next day.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What were some of the other bases that you'd go visit?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, boy. I don't have all that information with me.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: But there were other Air Force bases in South Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you keep in touch with any of the guys that you were friends with?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: After I -- well, before -- before I got out of service, I got together with a bunch of fellows, and we had a little get-together at the NCO club in -- let's see. Where was that in? I think it was at Chanute Air Force Base. I ran into four or five different master sergeants and tech sergeants. We had a little party at the NCO club and talked about old things and what they were doing, things like that and what they were doing down at Tan Son Nhut.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Was there any kind of entertainment for the servicemen while you were over in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. A couple times, we had -- we had a big theater out there. And every night, they would have something out there. And usually on a Friday or a Saturday night, we'd have a big band come out and entertain us. They had a -- it was a big studio that they built in -- at Tan Son Nhut.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you live right on the base?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I -- I lived on -- in a tent.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: In a tent?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: On the base because there was no families allowed.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: When your wife was there, where did you live? Did she live in the tent, too?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No, no. See, I don't think I got that pa -- that information with me. I had a list of all the houses -- all the addresses I've had in the service and out of the service for 25 years. I didn't remember finding that paper because Joe and Al Santucci went through my paperwork. They said, "Oh, you don't need this. You don't need that." The rest of it's all back at the VA hospital.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, well, I'll tell Joe. When he comes back, I'll tell him to make me a copy of that because it will show where you lived.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: If he can find it.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: If -- when your wife was there, were you on-base or off-base?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, I think the only time that my wife was with me where we was on the base was at Dover Air Force Base. And I put three times -- three tours out at Dover. And we always had base housing. And I raised two children there at Dover. That's another time -- another place where I worked at the NCO club as a bartender or a waiter. I always kept myself busy. Sometimes I'd put 12, 14 hours out on the flight line and go home and clean up and go to work at the -- at the NCO club.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: (inaudible)

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, money wasn't that good at that time, you know. You couldn't stretch your -- your monthly pay more than two or three weeks sometimes. Most of the people would go out and get odd lot jobs that they could stretch their dollar bill.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So when you worked at the officers club or did bartending or waiting, that was extra pay --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- on top of your service pay?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you get to see the Bob Hope show at all or any of the entertainers?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I think I saw Bob Hope someplace. I think it was at -- I think it was at Vietnam, the air base there. But I know I saw Bob Hope and his -- his crew come over for a nightly visit. I'm pretty sure it was at Tan Son Nhut.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember what that was like?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: He had a big concert?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, it had -- they had a lot of musicians there, but it wasn't really a concert deal. It was just gags and, you know, fun and dancing and stuff like that. There was only some seating out away from the stage that they had built for entertainment at that time. And we'd sit out in the back part on benches.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you have any pictures from when you were in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Any what?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Pictures?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I had some pictures, but I was told that you didn't want them.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: No. I do. But I'll get back in touch with you. If you have them and you can find them, I'd like to make copies of them.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you recall any humorous or funny stories?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, I can't remember back that far.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: My mind is going and my hearing is going. I thought -- I normally wear two hearing aids, and both of them are in the shop for repair.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I've been without hearing aids now for three weeks.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: That must be tough.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah, it is.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you keep a personal diary while you were --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Not really. No.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you remember your last days in Vietnam before you were shipped back home?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Not too much because there wasn't too much doing -- going on over there, you know, where I could remember about.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Was it the end -- do you remember the years you were there in Vietnam? Was it the beginning or the end of the war?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It was the end of my war -- the end of my period there. I was almost -- in fact, when I come back from Vietnam, I went to McChord Air Force Base in Washington -- in the state of Washington to retire.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Then you must have been older when you were in Vietnam. How old were you?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I was in -- I was in Vietnam -- 10 or 11 months in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And when you came home to the United States, did you retire from the Air Force at that time?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. I retired from McChord Air Force Base in Wash -- the state of Washington.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Did you come home from Vietnam first or your son?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. He was still in the service when I retired, and his ship come back from Vietnam in -- they docked at -- they docked in New York someplace. I forget the station. But my wife and I both went down and met his ship when the ship landed in -- in New York. We were stationed in Connecticut, I think, at the time. I was living in Connecticut.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: When you retired from McChord in Washington, what did you do after that? Or where did you go?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I don't remember. I know I wasn't out of -- I wasn't out of the service too much -- too long when I got a work -- when I went to work for Pratt & Whitney in Middletown, Connecticut as a machine operator. And I used to balance the parts before the parts were put into the engine. I used to run a balance machine. And I used to balance all the big fan blades, all the big fans for these C-124s, 29s and all these new airplanes they've got now. Big enormous, enormous big fans.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: That's okay. Have you seen a lot of change in the aircrafts --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- since you first started out?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. I'll say. I wouldn't recognize half the planes anymore.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: You don't think so?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: How did you end up in Connecticut from Washington?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: We -- when I come back from -- from -- when I retired, I went back to Massachusetts, Dracut, Massachusetts, where my wife was living. And we stayed there for about six months or so. And then we relocated and went back to -- I forget where we went back to, Connecticut or something. Been a long time.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And then how long did you work at Pratt & Whitney before you retired from there?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I retired on a -- on a medical. I put in almost nine years at Pratt & Whitney, but they wouldn't retire me as a long-time employment -- employee. They retired me medically. And I don't get nothing from Pratt & Whitney. I got one big check when I got -- when I retired, and that's it. I don't get no retirement pay from Pratt & Whitney.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow. What did you do after you retired from Pratt & Whitney?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: You stayed in Connecticut.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I'm trying to think. Well, I put 25 years at the -- at the VA hospital, I know.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. I was a volunteer driver for the drivers department.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: At the VA hospital in Newington, Connecticut?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: In Newington, yeah. Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Was that volunteer work or they paid you?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. They didn't pay me. No. It was all volunteer.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: This was after you retired from Pratt & Whitney?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: The only thing I got out of that -- out of that trip is I had a free lunch every day. That's all they give you is a free $4 lunch.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And what would you do? Drive -- pick up --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Pick up patients in my own car. I didn't even drive the VA vans. So I used my own car. I wore out three cars.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, my heavens. John, you've done a lot of stuff in your life.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. I've got -- I've got medals on my other cap. In fact, I left it -- left that cap in my car back in -- at the VA hospital, with all the ribbons and everything that I got from -- from services I've performed in the last 20-some years.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow. Did you join any veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I belong to the American Legion in Connecticut. I belong to the VFW in Connecticut. I belong to the DAV in Connecticut. What other one? I think I -- I think I'm still a member of the Elks in Connecticut also.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow. You're in a lot of organizations. Have you had any reunions since you got out of the service?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Not reunions, no, but the DAV is the one I'm proactive in, and we have big state meetings and conventions once a year, and we --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And you're still active in the DAV?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes, I am. I'm a service officer with the DAV, state DAV. I'm a chaplain for the -- chapter DAV in Bristol. I'm the chaplain. I've got four more months of that before I'll be out of that.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What are your duties as chaplain?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: All you do is -- that's a very simple job. You open -- all the meetings, you open the -- you open the meeting with a prayer for the beginning of the service, and then when all the paperwork is taken care of during the meeting, then we have a closing prayer, salute the flag, and the meeting's over. They're usually 35, 40 minutes, it's over with.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And that's once a month?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. That's the first Tuesday of every month. Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And where do you go for that?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Right in the DAV in Bristol.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And what does D-A-V stand for?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Disabled American Veterans.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: What other activities do you do with either the VFW or the DAV?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I don't do anything for the other ones anymore. I used to call bingo for the VFW in Plainville, but I had a conflict with some of the other officials of the club, and I quit doing it. I had -- I had a concern where I caught some people stealing money, and I got in trouble over that. And they didn't like me for reporting them, and you know, they wanted you to keep your mouth shut, you know. You were doing something wrong, and I saw it, and I told people about it, and you got the word after I did -- after I passed it out.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So are you still -- what do you do now for activities?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I'm still the obituary officer at the DA -- the DAV in Bristol. I check the newspapers every day, see if there's any of our members that died, you know, in the paper every day. And then if it is one of our members that died and his burial is not going to be for a day or two, then I usually go to the -- the -- not the cem -- to the funeral parlor and say a little prayer for the member that died, place a forget-me-not on his chest, salute him and then go back and shake hands with all his family members and things like that.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And you do this yourself?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I've been doing this for 20 years.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And you go to every one of them?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Every one of them for the DAV.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, my gosh. You must have been to a lot of them.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. I've been to enormous.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Now, when you go through the obits in the papers, do you look for Air Force guys?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. I just look for DAV members.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, do you have a big list? How do you know?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, we have -- we have a 900-page -- a 900-member book, membership book, which I'm due to get a new report in right now, this month. And I have to -- I have to number -- I have to number every -- every member's name so -- to put it in the book in place where it's supposed to be alphabetically. And then the old -- the old numbers, we just throw them away or pile them up in the office. We have an office next door, and it's a little part of the office that one of our -- what is his name? He's -- his name is Bill Shea, but he has a -- I forget what he's called. His -- all of his stuff is business, money. Stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Now, members of the Disabled Veterans, are they from all different branches of the service?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So it could be a Navy man that dies, and if he's in the DAV, you go?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you go alone or does a group of --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, if I can get a group to go with me, especially if it's a member that -- of the club that is an officer of the club. Then I'll ask three or four guys if they want to go down and pay their respects at the funeral home. And sometimes some of them will say, "Sure, I'll go." But any other time, I usually have to go down to a -- to a wake just by myself and say a little prayer and salute the patient and then walk out and show my respects to the family and present them -- I usually present them with a flag case, you know, after. If -- if the military man has got a flag over his casket and he's a member of our club, then he deserves the flag case. And I -- I go down to the engraver, which I have in Bristol, and he makes up the name, the person's name is -- and his date of death. And I put that on the front of the flag case before I present it to the family.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: That must mean a lot to the family.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It's a good keepsake. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: It must mean a lot to the families when they see another military man come, because I'm sure they don't expect that.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No, they don't. Yeah. Some of them don't. They say -- as you said, a lot of the people that -- even though they know that their husband was in the service and they belonged to the DAV, they don't know who's going to come represent the DAV. And this is my -- say 28th year I'm doing this, and I'm -- I'm going to quit after this -- this coming May, I'll be -- I'll be -- I'll have my 23rd year in as this obituary officer, and I'm just going to give it up. It's too much for me.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow. Well, you sure stay at things for a long time.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. Just going to the DAV every morning and -- and looking through the Bristol Press and the Hartford Courant to see if any of our members died is enough, but --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: You go every morning?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I go every day. Every day. Seven days a week.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Wow, that's really commitment.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. In fact, we just had a past commanders dinner Saturday night, and the commander that we have right now, he gave me a big award for the service that I do for the -- for the club. And I donated a thousand dollars towards the renovation of the bar. And they made a big thing out of that. And everybody gave me a big round of applause. And I just talked to them through the microphone and asked that there's so many people around here that I'm sure that they could be a little bit more easier with their money and add to this here fund that I've started here to renovate this bar. And they just clapped and said, "Yeah. Yeah. We'll see." Nobody --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: So you started it, huh?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Nobody me but a sucker.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: (laughter) Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or the military?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Did my military?

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Experience influence the way you think about the war or about military?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No, not really because I tried not to talk about it. I don't -- I don't tell everybody about my experiences of where I was and things like that.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, it's been so long since I got out of the service, I like to forget it. I know in the back of my mind, I can never forget what different things that I went through and different people I met and things like that, but I don't like the club -- the members of the club talking about me like that, making ex -- expressing their opinion of the things that I do and what I've been doing around the club. I try to keep my mouth shut.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: How did you feel about your son -- did only one son join the military?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yes. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And were you in favor of that? How did you feel about him joining?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: It was all right. I was -- I was surprised to hear that he did enlist in the Coast Guard and that he was going to be a radio technician. So he's a pretty smart fellow anyway. In fact, he's a retired police captain from Hartford right now. Hartford police department. He lives in Florida.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Why did he pick the Coast Guard and not the Air Force?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I don't know. I don't know. I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: How did the military affect your life? Because you spent a lot of your life in the military.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, I don't have no complaints about how the -- how I was treated at the military, in the services, the time I was in. I thought it was a privilege and an honor for me to be representing the Air Force and things like that and talk about different experiences of the time that I spent. A lot of times, I don't like to talk about it. It all depends on the mood I'm in.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Are you happy that you picked the Air Force?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I was happy. Because I didn't want to be in the Army. I didn't want to go in the Army.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I don't know. I just didn't care for the -- the training I was watching on TV before I even went in the service. I just never --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Have you seen a big change in the Air Force from when you first enlisted and from when you retired?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. I don't -- I don't believe that there's anything that I -- that I see different that's going on that was in -- going on when I was there. I know that they're doing a lot -- got a lot of women in now in the service and that women are doing very good on their rank and privileges and things like that. It seemed like they're a lot smarter than they were 25, 30 years ago. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And so right now, you're retired. And are you living alone?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I'm alone.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And your daughter and your son are nearby. And it sounds like you still stay pretty active in the DAV.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I have -- I have a daughter that lives in New Hampshire, and my -- my youngest son lives in Southington. And my oldest son lives in Miami, Florida.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: And you're still very active at your young age. When are you going to slow down?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: The day that they say, "God bless you. You did a good job."

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: The day I die. That's probably when I'll quit. I was threatening to quit, as I said, this year, but my commander says, "No. You're not going to quit on me."

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: "When I get out of service, you can do anything you want to, but not while I'm -- not while I'm commander. You're not going to quit." He just gave me -- gave me that alternative.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: As an officer, because you were a staff -- a master sergeant?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Master sergeant.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: How was your life different as an officer than the enlisted men underneath you?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, I don't -- I don't know any difference, but the high-ranking officers and the -- and the enlisted men that worked for me, under me, I always got along good with them. I'd ask a guy to do something and, "Sure. If I can do it, I can do it." Very cooperative and I got along good with the people that worked for me. I tried to keep active with the -- with the officers and people that are above me also.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Is there anything else that you would like to add that we haven't covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, the only other thing is that I spent 25 years as -- as a VA volunteer for the DAV hospital, for the VA hospital. I have -- my last dona -- my last award was a 4,000-hour pin for driving my car, bringing the patients to the hospital.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: 4,000 hours?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: 4,000 hours.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: That's a lot. You certainly have given a huge hunk of your life and lots of --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: That's right. I have.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- time.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: In fact, we've got a DAV meeting coming up next month, I think it is, in Rocky Hill. No. In Meriden. Some restaurant. We usually have a place to go to (inaudible) restaurant, eating place. That's -- sometimes 20 or 30 people show up to the meetings. I haven't gone to any DAV national meetings yet because I can never get time or the money to go to travel around, the expense of just going to the meeting. And then the meeting lasts three days, and you've got to stay in a hotel, in a motel. Another 150 bucks right there, you know. I try and stretch my money the best I can. I make -- I make good money, but I mean, I -- I get it from the government, but I have other expenses that I have to take care of before I can take care of myself.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: If you had it to do all over again, would you do it the same way? Make the military your career?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I'm not sure. Not being that much active with the -- with the -- with the military as I used to be, I don't know whether or not I could take some of the things that they ask you to do nowadays. I believe that I did my share, and I did the best I could, and I got rewarded for it. And that's all I need.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Is there anything else that you can recall that you'd like to add?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: No. I think I've given you just about everything that I've been involved in between the DAV and the VA hospital. I don't -- I don't do much -- my other office -- other units or veterans organizations that I -- that I belong to, I don't -- I'm not very active in them anymore, but I'm strictly -- strictly right now a DAV full-time member, you know, full-time troublemaker. I go down there every day and sit down and read the papers and read all the obituaries. And I take care of the bathrooms. I clean up the bathrooms. I fill up all the toilet paper, towels and paper towels and keep all the supplies in stock that we use normally during the day or week. And --

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Do you think you could still work on an airplane?

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Well, being that so many of them are jets now, I don't think I'd want to work on jets because I'm sure that they're as complicated working on as they are when I was watching them being built in Pratt & Whitney because -- too complicated.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Well, I'd like to thank you for --

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I hope I gave you enough.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: -- allowing me to interview you, John.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: I hope I gave you enough information that you want.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Yes, you have. I appreciate it. I think it's an honor and a privilege for me to be able to talk to somebody who's given as much as you have for our country.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Eileen M. Hurst
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: John Wolf
sp.p: Thank you. (End of interview)
